paragraphs: Decision center: The work of a disc jockey other than radio is to turn front-end conditions such as client and venue expectations, the preferences and mood of the live crowd, and equipment and music material into a live music service that is visible, clearly audible and reviewable by the organizer — first communicate activity information with the client or venue manager (music preferences, schedule, expected attendance and segments), then prepare equipment and the music library and customize the playlist by activity segment, then complete equipment assembly and sound check and appearance confirmation, then during the event select tracks and mix in response to the crowd and build the mood and take song requests, and finally collect payment, issue an itemized invoice and review and hand off. The focus of judgment is not whether you can play songs, but whether every step of the communication—preparation—check—execution—closing chain holds the boundaries of equipment and electrical safety, lawful use of music and copyright, and time and contract and charges.

Good to try first: Willing to communicate repeatedly among clients, venue managers and the live crowd and accept last-minute changes; able to turn music preferences, activity segments and timelines into an executable playback and equipment plan; able to maintain equipment and sound quality under noise, lighting and crowd interference; able to accept a schedule mainly of evenings, weekends and holidays, and to work according to contract and invoice and charging processes.

Proceed with caution: If you expect this job to be mainly choosing and playing your own songs, or you are unwilling to handle client communication and contracts and invoices and equipment transport and sound checks, or you find it hard to accept irregular hours and fierce competition and a noisy environment, or you equate knowing how to use playback software with being allowed to ignore music copyright and requirements for equipment electricity and venue safety, then the actual work experience usually does not match the expectation.

Low-risk verification: Using the fictional activity, venue and music library materials provided on this page, complete a paper exercise of arranging a two-hour playlist by activity segment, listing an equipment and check list, and writing a quote and settlement statement. This only verifies whether you are willing to check off client needs, time, equipment and compliance conditions item by item and record truthfully. The exercise uses fictional materials, does not involve real clients, venues or musical works, makes no performance or charging commitments, and is not equivalent to equipment operation training or practice qualification.

Decision center: Whether client and venue expectations and live crowd preferences can be organized into a live music service chain that can be executed from communication to closing and reviewed by the organizer.

Work is mainly in a controlled indoor setting with irregular schedules and extensive contact with people: decision freedom very much 72%, use email every day 63%, dealing with external customers or the public extremely important 60%, working hours irregular 60%, telephone conversations weekly or more 50%, public speaking weekly or more 48%, time pressure weekly or more 44%, continuous use of hands 44%, contact with others most of the time 44%, continuous standing 36%, exposure to distracting or uncomfortable noise weekly or more 32%, level of competition extremely fierce 40%. The workplace is weddings, banquets, commercial events and entertainment venues, and the rhythm is determined by the event schedule and client needs.

Similar names do not mean the same duties: This page is O*NET-SOC 27-2091.00 Disc Jockeys, Except Radio. Adjacent positions have different duties — broadcast hosts and radio disc jockeys host programs inside broadcasting organizations and are bound by the director and the broadcasting rules, musicians and singers perform live music by playing and singing, audio engineering technicians are responsible for setting up and tuning and maintaining sound reinforcement systems, and meeting and convention and event planners are responsible for overall event planning and suppliers and budgets. The focus of this occupation is paid music and mood services for clients and live crowds: equipment operation and track selection and mixing, sequencing by activity segment, mood building and taking song requests, and contracts and invoices and promotion. Requirements such as the qualification of commercial performance operating entities, venue and electricity and fire safety, music copyright use and the protection of minors are governed by the laws of the relevant jurisdiction and the organizer's rules, and are not inferred from the job title.

Inputs that must be checked: the activity type and flow and timeline, the client's and venue's music and atmosphere and do-not-play requirements, venue electricity and load-bearing and access and noise limits, the equipment list and backup plan, requirements for the use of musical works and copyright, the quote and contract and charging method, and the organizer's and venue's safety and admission rules. What must not be done: do not use unlicensed musical works for public playback or recording or dissemination, do not set up equipment without confirming electricity and load-bearing and access conditions, do not make service commitments to clients beyond the contract, do not take over the organizer's safety and emergency command duties, and do not disclose information about clients, guests or venues.

The fit judgment should be made by considering whether you can communicate effectively with clients and venues, whether you can turn preferences and segments into an executable playback plan, whether you can maintain equipment and sound quality under noise and interference, whether you can accept irregular hours and competition, and whether you are clear about the boundaries of music copyright and equipment and venue safety; it should not be replaced by a self-assessment of having many saved playlists or often playing music at friends' gatherings; all of these must be confirmed in supervised actual events and a trial.

All exercises on this page use fictional materials; real public playback of musical works, commercial performance operation, venue electricity and fire protection and temporary stage and grandstand erection, and professional sound reinforcement and lighting equipment operation must be carried out by persons who have obtained the corresponding qualifications according to law or who are authorized by the organizer and venue side, in accordance with applicable laws and rules; the use of musical works must comply with copyright and collective management requirements. Individuals may not hold commercial performances on their own or make external charging commitments, and this page does not constitute performance management, copyright, safety or tax advice.

The work object of this occupation is music and mood services at live events: clients and venue managers, the activity flow and timeline, the sites of weddings and banquets and commercial events and entertainment venues, sound reinforcement and playback and lighting and visual equipment, music material and playlists, and live guests and song requests. The output is a live music service that keeps the event moving smoothly according to the timeline: a music and atmosphere plan confirmed with the client, a playlist ordered by activity segment, equipment and cabling assembled and checked, live playback and mood building adjusted to the crowd response, and quotes and contracts and itemized invoices and settlement records. The basis for judgment is the activity flow and timeline and client requirements, the venue's electricity and load-bearing and access and noise limits, the technical requirements and backup plan for equipment, the requirements for the use of musical works and copyright, and the organizer's and venue's safety and admission rules — not personal preference or job title.

Judgment one: Are activity needs clearly checked — do you first confirm the activity type and flow and timeline, the music and atmosphere and do-not-play requirements, and the expected attendance and key segments with the client or venue manager, rather than copying your own usual playlist?

Judgment two: Is the playback and equipment plan executable — is the playlist with backup tracks arranged by activity segment and timeline, and does the equipment match the venue electricity and space and load-bearing and have a backup plan?

Judgment three: Are equipment assembly and sound check in place — is the equipment assembled and wired and secured to standard, and have the sound check and channel and volume confirmation been completed with emergency handling prepared?

Judgment four: Does live execution follow the timeline and respond to the crowd — does it proceed according to the flow, adjusting track selection and mood according to crowd response and song requests, while holding the do-not-play and volume and venue limits?

Judgment five: Are music use and equipment and venue safety held — does the use of musical works meet licensing requirements, are electricity and cabling and equipment securing and access safe, and are anomalies handled or reported immediately?

Judgment six: Are the quote and contract and settlement clear — do the quote and contract state the scope of service and duration and equipment and fees, and is the agreed charge collected after the event with an itemized invoice issued and records kept?

The work of disc jockeys other than radio can be divided into three connected but independent work areas. The first is needs communication and plan preparation: communicate activity information and music preferences and schedule and expected attendance with the client or venue manager, customize the playlist by activity segment, prepare music material and backup tracks, and prepare equipment and venue adaptation plans. The second is equipment assembly and live execution: assemble and wire and secure audio, video and lighting equipment, complete sound checks and volume and channel confirmation, move the event forward according to the timeline while selecting tracks and mixing and building mood in response to the crowd, take song requests and operate lighting and visual effects and write announcement scripts. The third is closing and business matters: dismantle and inventory equipment, collect fees, issue itemized invoices and write booking contracts, promote services through internet advertising and brochures, and review the live event and client feedback before handing off. All three work areas proceed within client requirements, venue conditions and legal and institutional boundaries.

When doing this job, which judgments are most prone to error, and how should they be checked?

Common errors cluster into four categories: first, needs are not clearly asked and the playlist follows personal habit, causing do-not-play violations or segment misalignment; second, equipment and venue do not match or checks are inadequate, causing silence and feedback and power loss on site; third, on site people focus only on playing songs and ignore the timeline and crowd response and venue limits; fourth, charges and contracts and invoices are not documented as agreed. The checking method is that each item has a reviewable basis: needs confirmation records and playlists, equipment and venue check lists, sound check and volume records, on-site timelines and song request records, and quotes and contracts and invoices — not impressions or improvised handling.

This table compares disc jockeys other than radio with six adjacent positions that are easily confused within live performance and event content or that have rotation and transfer relationships, row by row by core work and outputs, key differences, and basis for choice. The purpose of the comparison is not to rank them, but to explain their respective responsibility boundaries and scope of authorization — in particular that commercial performance operating qualifications, sound reinforcement system engineering, copyright use of musical works, and overall event safety and budget responsibility cannot all be assumed by this occupation.

Three things should govern the comparison: first, the work object (live crowd and client expectations, programs and broadcasting, works and playing and singing, sound reinforcement systems and acoustics, overall event plans and budgets); second, the basis and authorization (the activity flow and client requirements, the programming and directing rules of broadcasting organizations, scores and rehearsals and performance arrangements, system design and equipment manuals, and the applicability of each of the contracts and supplier and venue rules); third, outputs and responsibility (who is responsible for the live music service, who is responsible for program broadcasting, who is responsible for the performance presentation, who is responsible for the safety and sound quality of the sound reinforcement system, and who is responsible for the overall safety and budget of the event). Where the three are inconsistent, the position's actual duties and the organizer's and venue's authorization documents govern.

The basis for choice can follow three lines: if you want to provide paid music and mood services for clients and live crowds and personally operate equipment and select tracks, the occupation on this page is the closest fit; if you want to host programs inside a broadcasting organization, you should follow the broadcast host and radio disc jockey path and check the broadcasting and directing rules; if you want to do technical work around sound reinforcement systems and acoustics, an audio engineering technician is more suitable; if you prefer overall event planning and supplier and budget management, meeting and convention and event planner is another path. When transferring between positions, what must be filled in is object knowledge, technical training and scope of authorization, not just equipment proficiency.

Boundaries and sources: the differences listed in this table are based on the O*NET occupation profiles and work context data for each occupation, and on the Chinese mainland Regulations on the Administration of Commercial Performances (promulgated by State Council Decree No. 439 of 2005, revised for the fourth time by State Council Decree No. 732 on 2020-11-29) and the Implementing Rules for the Regulations on the Administration of Commercial Performances (Ministry of Culture Decree No. 47, revised in 2022) regarding the qualifications of commercial performance operating entities and performance approval and filing. The qualification and authorization requirements of adjacent positions cannot substitute for one another; this page does not infer income levels or hiring conditions from job titles, nor does it read live music service duties as commercial performance operating qualifications or sound reinforcement system engineering responsibility.

Present musical works to audiences by playing instruments or singing, and take responsibility for intonation, rhythm, style and stage presentation.

Objects and responsibility differ: musicians and singers are responsible for the artistic presentation of works and for live playing and singing; the occupation on this page serves clients and crowds by playing and mixing and building mood, and does not bear the artistic responsibility for performing or singing works.

If you want to make playing and singing your career and go deep into works and the stage, you can follow the musician and singer path and check training and performance opportunities; if you would rather operate equipment and select tracks around client needs and the live mood, the occupation on this page is a closer fit.
Broadcast hosts and radio disc jockeys (27-3011.00)
Host programs inside a broadcasting organization, link content and announce information, and complete the broadcast according to broadcasting rules and the director's instructions.

Scenarios and basis differ: broadcast hosts and radio disc jockeys work inside broadcasting organizations and the broadcasting system and are responsible for program content and broadcast compliance; the occupation on this page faces live clients and crowds and is responsible for the live music service and equipment and charges, and does not bear broadcasting and content review responsibility.

If you want to enter a broadcasting organization for program hosting, you can follow the broadcast host and radio disc jockey path and check announcing and content compliance requirements; if you want to do live event music services, the occupation on this page is more suitable.
Audio engineering technicians (27-4014.00)

Technical responsibility differs: audio engineering technicians are responsible for the design, setup, tuning and testing of sound reinforcement systems; the occupation on this page is responsible for live playback and track selection and mood and contract charges, and complex sound reinforcement system and electrical and acoustic problems should be transferred to professionals.

If you prefer technical work with equipment and acoustics, you can follow the audio engineering technician direction and receive systematic training; if you want to face clients and crowds directly with music services, the occupation on this page is a closer fit.
Meeting, convention and event planners (13-1121.00)

Scope and responsibility differ: meeting and convention and event planners are responsible for overall event planning and suppliers and budgets and on-site coordination; the occupation on this page provides the music and mood service segment within that, and does not bear overall planning and supplier and budget and safety command responsibility.

If you want to coordinate the overall event plan and budget and suppliers, you can choose the meeting and convention and event planner direction; if you want to focus on live music and mood, the occupation on this page is more suitable.
Lighting technicians (27-4015.00)

Professional division of labor differs: lighting technicians are responsible for lighting design and equipment and effects; the occupation on this page may also operate lighting and visual effects equipment, but is mainly a music service, and complex lighting design and safety should be borne by professionals.

If you prefer lighting and visual design and equipment operation, you can choose the lighting technician direction and receive specialized training; if you want music and mood as the main line, the occupation on this page is more suitable.

If you want to make performance your career, you can follow the actor path; if you want to work around live music and mood and client service, the occupation on this page is more suitable.

China's Copyright Law as amended in 2020: Article 10 distinguishes the rights of performance, reproduction, broadcasting and online communication; Articles 26 and 29 require licenses to be checked by right, territory and period; Article 38 provides that the organizer of a performance obtains the license for the work and pays remuneration, with performers and organizers checked according to the actual situation. Article 45 provides that playing a sound recording to the public with equipment requires payment to the producer of the sound recording; reproduction and online communication are checked separately against Article 44 concerning the rights in works and of performers. The rights in works, sound recordings and performances are checked separately, and purchasing a file or a personal subscription does not automatically include commercial public playback, reproduction or dissemination; collective management is one route to authorization and it is not the case that association licensing is the only option. Observation signal one: is willing to first ask clearly about client and venue needs and segments and do-not-play requirements before arranging the playlist, rather than opening according to personal preference.
Observation signal two: can treat equipment and electricity and cabling and backup plans as hard requirements, assembling to standard and completing a sound check, rather than improvising on site.
Observation signal three: can maintain equipment and timeline and sound quality under noise, lighting and crowd interference, and adjust to on-site reactions without losing the flow.
Observation signal four: can accept evenings and weekends and holidays and irregular schedules, and work according to contract and quote and invoice and settlement processes.

Trainable abilities include needs communication and playlist arrangement, equipment assembly and cabling and sound checks and tuning, mixing and track transitions and mood building, lighting and visual equipment operation, contracts and quotes and invoices and promotion, and copyright and venue safety requirements.

The workload includes continuous standing and hand operation, irregular hours and night travel, high-frequency interpersonal contact and public speaking, time pressure and a noisy environment, and the cost and schedule pressure of working independently.

Counter-signals include expecting the work to be mainly choosing and playing your own songs, being unwilling to handle client communication and equipment transport and contracts and invoices, finding irregular schedules and fierce competition and a noisy environment hard to accept, or equating knowing how to use playback software with being allowed to ignore music licensing and electricity and venue safety requirements.

items.title: Training, authorization and commercial performance operation boundaries

paragraphs: Entering the disc jockey other than radio direction is not just taking a course; first check the scope of duties for bookings and event opportunities, equipment and venue conditions, and music licensing and commercial performance operation and filing requirements.
Stage one: use fictional activity and music library materials to practice needs confirmation, playlist arrangement, equipment and check lists, and quote and settlement statements.
Stage two: complete limited tasks in supervised events, keeping supervisor and client feedback and correction records.

values: Fictional materials

Fictional activities (one two-hour wedding banquet and one three-hour commercial promotion), client requirements and do-not-play lists, venue electricity and load-bearing and access condition descriptions, music library list (60 tracks, with era and style tags) and equipment list.
All materials are fictional and contain no real client, guest or musical work information.
Portfolio task

Within 60 minutes, complete the playlist for a two-hour event (in five segments: opening, speeches, dining, celebration, send-off) and backup tracks, an equipment and sound check list, and a quote and settlement statement (including overtime and equipment and transport scope).
Do paper checking and plan design only; do not contact real clients, venues or musical works, and make no performance or charging commitments.
Reference result

Each of the five segments has style and rhythm and volume requirements; the playlist includes 2 do-not-play replacements and 4 backup tracks; the equipment list covers primary and backup and cabling and power and securing and access and noise prompts; the quote states duration and overtime and equipment and transport and settlement method and marks items pending confirmation.
The reference result is for self-checking and is not the only correct answer.
Boundary statement

The exercise is for career exploration and does not constitute equipment operation qualifications, commercial performance operating qualifications, performance approval or copyright licensing; real events must be carried out by trained personnel and under entity and venue conditions that have obtained the corresponding qualifications according to law or are authorized, and must not proceed without authorization when public music playback and electricity and setup are involved.

items.title: Entry case material: a fictional playlist and equipment check

values: Day 1: understand the materials
Read the fictional activity and client requirements and venue conditions and music library list, circle uncertain items and write out a question list.
Day 2: needs and playlist
Arrange the two-hour playlist and backup tracks by the five segments, marking do-not-play replacements and volume and rhythm requirements.
Day 3: equipment and checks
List the equipment and cabling and power and securing and access and noise check list and backup plan.
Day 4: licensing and compliance
Write out the check items and responsible parties for the use of musical works and commercial performance operation and filing and venue admission.
Day 5: quote and settlement
Complete the quote and settlement statement, stating duration and overtime and equipment and transport and settlement cycle and items pending confirmation.
Day 6: timed redo
Redo a version under time limits and record your energy and the types of errors.
Day 7: compare and decide
Compare the two versions of the plan and write down continue / proceed with caution / stop and the reasons.

entries: Day 1 judgment: whether uncertain items in the materials were truthfully marked rather than filled in by guesswork.
Day 2 judgment: whether the playlist is arranged by segment and client requirements, and whether do-not-play replacements and backup tracks are stated.
Day 3 judgment: whether the equipment and check list covers electricity and securing and access and noise and backup plans.
Day 4 judgment: whether the licensing and compliance check items state the responsible parties, rather than assuming one may hold the event on one's own.
Day 5 judgment: whether the quote and settlement state duration and overtime and equipment and transport and the settlement cycle.
Day 6 judgment: whether safety and authorization and client requirements can still be held under time limits.
Day 7 judgment: combining the performance in both versions, judge whether you are willing to keep investing in the live music service direction.

facts.display_value: Note: the Chinese mainland has no unified occupational qualification corresponding one-to-one with United States 27-2091.00. Holding a commercial performance requires an entity that has obtained a commercial performance operating license according to law to apply to the competent culture department of the county-level people's government where the performance is held, under the Regulations on the Administration of Commercial Performances (promulgated by State Council Decree No. 439 of 2005, revised for the fourth time by State Council Decree No. 732 on 2020-11-29); performances involving foreign countries or Hong Kong, Macao or Taiwan apply to the provincial level or to the competent culture department of the State Council. Performance venue operating units, and individual performers and individual performance brokers who take commercial performance as their profession, should register according to law and file with the competent culture department of the county-level people's government where they are located within 20 days from the date of obtaining the business license; the Implementing Rules for the Regulations on the Administration of Commercial Performances (Ministry of Culture Decree No. 47, revised in 2022) provide that an application to hold a commercial performance should generally submit materials 3 days before the performance date, and 20 days before for performances involving foreign countries or Hong Kong, Macao or Taiwan; performances with temporarily erected stages and grandstands must also comply with the Regulations on the Safety Management of Large Mass Activities and require acceptance documents; publicly playing or disseminating musical works must meet copyright and collective management requirements. Practitioners related to this occupation are mostly freelancers settled per event or per contract, or employed by venues and events, and public wage statistics are broken down at most to industry category and unit type, with no occupation-level scope corresponding to this occupation established, so no verifiable Chinese mainland occupation-level wage distribution was obtained in this round

description.text: Disc Jockeys, Except Radio (O*NET-SOC 27-2091.00) provide paid music and mood services at weddings, banquets, commercial events and entertainment venues: confirm music preferences and schedule and activity segments with the client, customize the playlist by segment, assemble equipment and do a sound check, select tracks and mix and build mood and take song requests according to the timeline, operate lighting and visual equipment and write and make announcements, and complete quotes and contracts and itemized invoices and settlement and review. United States scope: the BLS 2025 wage data hourly median is 21.61 US dollars (hourly percentiles 13.50／16.91／21.61／37.50／60.17 US dollars; that source does not publish an annual scope); employment was about 15,400 in 2024, with growth of 3% to 4% in 2024—2034 and about 1,500 projected openings; the preparation level is Job Zone 1-2 and the interest code is AEC. subject.name: Disc Jockeys, Except Radio
subject.summary: Disc Jockeys, Except Radio (United States side, O*NET-SOC 27-2091.00) is a position providing paid music and mood services for clients and live crowds: operating disc jockey controllers and microphones and other audio and video equipment, communicating activity information with clients or venue managers (music preferences, schedule, expected attendance), customizing the playlist by activity segment, assembling audio and video equipment and doing a sound check, selecting tracks and playing and mixing according to crowd preferences and mood, taking guest song requests, operating lighting and smoke and visual equipment and building mood and hosting party games, writing announcement scripts and booking contracts, issuing itemized invoices and promoting services through internet advertising and brochures; and after the event dismantling and inventorying equipment, collecting fees and reviewing and handing off. United States scope: for this occupation the BLS 2025 wage data hourly median is 21.61 US dollars, with hourly percentiles of 13.50／16.91／21.61／37.50／60.17 US dollars; that source publishes only the hourly scope for this occupation and does not publish an annual median wage or annual percentiles, and this page does not convert them on its own. The O*NET summary page gives employment of about 15,400 in 2024, growth of 3% to 4% in 2024—2034 (average) and about 1,500 projected job openings; the preparation level is Job Zone 1-2 (SVP below 6.0), the education feedback is 52% high school or equivalent and 36% less than high school and 4% some college no degree, with on-the-job training from a few days to a year; the interest code is AEC; the work context includes decision freedom very much 72%, use email every day 63%, dealing with external customers or the public extremely important 60%, working hours irregular 60%, public speaking weekly or more 48%, continuous standing 36%, continuous use of hands 44%, noise exposure weekly or more 32%, and level of competition extremely fierce 40%. Chinese mainland scope: this occupation has no uniform access-type individual certificate; holding a commercial performance requires an entity that has obtained a commercial performance operating license according to law to apply for approval under the Regulations on the Administration of Commercial Performances (promulgated by State Council Decree No. 439 of 2005, revised for the fourth time by State Council Decree No. 732 on 2020-11-29) and its implementing rules, and performance venue operating units and individual performers and individual performance brokers must file as prescribed; publicly playing or disseminating musical works must meet copyright and collective management requirements. Public statistics have not established an occupation-level wage scope corresponding to this occupation, and this page truthfully retains the gap.
